Foreign body aspiration

Airway Foreign Body is when a foreign body (food or objects) enter the airway and either sit in the larynx or beyond in the trachea or bronchi

Airway foreign body is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality among children especially older infants and toddlers (60% of all airway foreign body cases)

Epidemiology

Males are 1.7 more likely affected than females

In infants younger than 6 months, the cause is usually secondary to feeding by a well meaning sibling

Most common aspirated FB are food items (70%): ex. Nuts, seeds, bread and meat, hard candy, gum, bones, raw fruits and vegetables; common inorganic objects aspirated (30%): coins, latex balloons, pins, jewelry, magnets, pen caps, and toys

Globular, compressible or round objects such as grapes, meat and bread, grapes, nuts, balloons, marshmallows and candies can block the airway completely, so they are very dangerous

Unlike inorganic objects, aspirated vegetable commonly causes intense pneumonitis and subsequent pneumonia and suppurative bronchitis.

Pathophysiology

Young children are more at risk to aspirate a FB because they often use their mouths to explore their surroundings and they are generally more likely to be distracted, playing or ambulatory while eating

Young children are more vulnerable to chocking because they have smaller airway diameter than adults

Clinical features

Clinical features are variable depending on the type, duration, and location of the FB

It ranges from asymptomatic to severe respiratory distress

The most serious complication is complete airway obstruction which manifest in the conscious child as sudden respiratory distress followed by inability to speak or cough

FB Aspiration result in symptoms divided into three stages:

Initial event: paroxysms of coughing, choking, gagging and maybe airway obstruction occur immediately after aspiration of FB, sometimes the child expel the FB during this stage

Asymptomatic interval: the FB becomes lodged, reflexes are fatigued, and immediate symptoms subsides. Lack of symptoms in this stage is deceiving and lead to delayed and missed diagnosis

Complications: airway obstruction, erosions, pneumonia and atelectasis develop which will manifest as fever, cough, hemoptysis …

A FB aspiration should be suspected if there is a history of sudden onset of coughing or choking and should be considered in all children with unilateral wheezing.

At presentation, many patients are in the asymptomatic interval

Classifications

Laryngotracheal FB: patient present with stridor and hoarseness with a FB in the laryngotracheal area

Bronchial FB: patient present with unilateral wheezing and decreased breath sounds with a bronchial FB.

Wheeze may be present in 30% of laryngotracheal FB aspirations and stridor in up to 10% of bronchial aspirations.

80% of FBs are in the bronchi.

Patients with immediate onset of severe stridor and cardiac arrest usually have laryngotracheal aspirations.

Diagnosis

Bronchoscopy is the gold standard for diagnosis and removal of the foreign body

History is the most important factor in determining the need for bronchoscopy, a positive history must never be ignored but a negative history can be misleading because FB aspiration can be missed and confused with more common causes of respiratory diseases because patients may have fever, wheezing, or rales

Child caregivers should be asked about nuts and seeds because they are the most common airway FBs

Examination of the nose, oral cavity, pharynx and lung sounds in important

Radiology also important, plain x rays are the first line, inspiratory PA chest is ordered first, expiratory or lateral decubitus films can assist in diagnosis

90% of FBs are radiolucent and not seen on x rays but secondary findings such as air trapping, asymmetric hyperinflation, obstructive emphysema, atelectasis, mediastinal shift and consolidation all important in identifying location of the FB

CT scan has no role in Airway foreign body due to radiation risk in pediatric population although it is highly sensitive and specific and able to detect radiolucent object

So if there is high index of suspicion despite negative or inconclusive imaging, bronchoscopy should be done

Upper esophageal FBs

Upper esophageal FBs are usually radiopaque and can impinge on the posterior aspect of the trachea.

Patients may present with stridor, and typically have dysphagia.

Radiographically, flat FBs such as coins are usually oriented in the sagittal plane when located in the trachea and in the coronal plane when in the esophagus.

Treatment

If FB aspiration or airway obstruction is clearly present, perform basic life support (BLS) procedures to relieve airway obstruction (back blows and abdominal thrusts)

If BLS maneuvers fail, perform direct laryngoscopy and extraction of the FB with Magill forceps. If the FB cannot be seen, orotracheal intubation with dislodgement of the FB distally may be lifesaving.

If an obstructive laryngotracheal FB cannot be removed or dislodged, an emergent surgical airway may be required.

Definitive treatment of partial airway obstruction usually requires rigid bronchoscopy in the operating room under general anesthesia by an otolaryngologist or pulmonologist

Complications of rigid bronchoscopy include bronchospasm, bleeding and airway edema
